**Memo**

To: Engineering Leadership  
From: Platform Engineering  
Date: [Date]  
Subject: Local AI capacity—utilization before expansion

We need to decide whether to buy more local AI hardware or to improve utilization of the capacity we already own. My recommendation is to defer a broad hardware purchase and commit to a focused, time-boxed utilization program, with a clear gate for targeted expansion if the evidence justifies it. The case for buying is intuitive because demand is visible and queueing is painful, but the case for utilization is stronger at our current scale because it is cheaper, faster to test, and far more reversible.

The cost of local AI hardware is not just the purchase price. It includes power, cooling, rack space, support, depreciation, and the engineering attention required to keep another failure domain healthy. Idle or poorly scheduled capacity is expensive even when it looks like headroom. Our likely inefficiencies are familiar: uneven per-model residency, small batch sizes, fragmented tenant quotas, caches that are not shared, and peak concurrency that forces overprovisioning for short windows. Software changes to scheduling, batching, model routing, quantization, and cache policy can recover meaningful capacity without new capital. That said, utilization work is not free. It consumes scarce engineering time, and that opportunity cost must be weighed against product work and against the cost of simply buying our way out of the problem.

Latency and reliability complicate the picture. Pushing utilization higher can increase queueing delay and make tail latency less predictable, especially for interactive workloads that share capacity with batch jobs. We should not treat “higher utilization” as an unconditional good. We need explicit service-level objectives, priority classes, admission control, and reserved headroom for failover. More hardware adds capacity but also adds failure domains, power and cooling risk, and operational burden for a small team. Better utilization can concentrate load and reduce redundancy if we are careless. The right target is not maximum utilization; it is predictable latency and reliable service at a defensible cost.

Reversibility should drive the sequencing. Scheduling policies, quotas, batching, caching, and quantization are software controls that we can tune, roll back, or narrow to specific workloads. A hardware purchase is much less reversible: it locks capital, space, and support commitments, and lead times may outlast the demand spike that motivated it. A cloud burst is more reversible than owned hardware but can be costly and introduces data-placement and operational complexity. Given uncertainty in workload forecasts, model changes, and latency sensitivity, we should prefer the reversible option until we have better evidence.

I recommend a six-to-eight-week utilization sprint with instrumentation as the first deliverable. We should measure per-model and per-tenant utilization, queue delay, rejection rates, cache hit rates, batch efficiency, and idle residency, then implement the highest-yield controls: fair scheduling, quotas, batching, model routing, quantization where quality allows, shared caching, and idle eviction. We should define latency and reliability SLOs before tuning, so we do not trade user experience for a utilization number. The purchase gate should be explicit: sustained high utilization during business hours, repeated SLO breaches caused by capacity rather than scheduling, rejected work that cannot be deferred, or a forecast that clearly exceeds post-improvement capacity. If a single bottleneck emerges, a small targeted expansion may be justified; a broad purchase is not.

There is real uncertainty here. Our utilization metrics may be incomplete, forecasts may be wrong, and some workloads may prove too latency-sensitive for aggressive sharing. That is exactly why the decision should be staged. My recommendation is to improve utilization first, keep a modest contingency for a targeted purchase, and revisit hardware once we have measured results. This approach protects cost, preserves latency and reliability, limits opportunity cost, and keeps the decision reversible.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Engineering Leadership  
**From:** Platform Engineering  
**Subject:** Local AI capacity: improve utilisation before expanding  
**Date:** [Date]

We need to decide whether to buy more local AI hardware or to get more useful capacity out of the equipment we already own. My recommendation is to defer additional local hardware purchases for one quarter and fund a bounded utilisation and reliability programme instead, with explicit technical and financial triggers for revisiting the purchase decision. I am not arguing that we will never need more hardware. I am arguing that we do not yet have enough evidence to justify adding fixed cost and operational complexity, and that the cheaper, more reversible work should come first.

The cost case is broader than the purchase price of accelerators. Local AI capacity carries power and cooling, rack space, support contracts, spares, firmware and driver maintenance, and depreciation. Idle or fragmented capacity is expensive even when it looks abundant on a dashboard. We should measure effective utilisation in terms of useful inference or training work completed per unit of cost, including memory pressure, queue wait, preemption, and stranded capacity from poor packing. If current utilisation is low or uneven, buying more hardware mostly adds fixed cost and consumes capital that could fund reliability work, observability, or other engineering priorities. The opportunity cost of engineering time matters too: a utilisation programme is not free, but it is usually cheaper and more reversible than a capital purchase.

Latency and reliability cut both ways. Better scheduling, admission control, batching, model routing, caching, and appropriate quantisation can raise throughput and reduce queueing delay without new hardware. But aggressive consolidation can erode headroom, increase tail latency, and enlarge the blast radius of failures. We should not chase nameplate utilisation at the expense of service-level objectives. More hardware can improve reliability through redundancy, but it also adds failure domains, firmware variance, and operational burden. A modest investment in health checks, draining, isolation, capacity buffers, and observability may improve reliability more than additional nodes. The right target is not maximum utilisation; it is predictable latency and failure behaviour under realistic load.

Reversibility strongly favours the utilisation path. Software, scheduling policy, and process changes can be rolled back or tuned. Hardware purchases are much less reversible: depreciation, procurement lead times, vendor lock-in, and physical installation all make a mistaken purchase costly to undo. A short cloud-burst or leased capacity arrangement for peak demand is also more reversible than expanding the local fleet, though it introduces data-egress, compliance, and cost-variability concerns that must be weighed explicitly. If demand is uncertain, preserving the option to buy later is valuable.

There is real uncertainty. Demand forecasts may be wrong, model mix may shift, vendor roadmaps may change, and our utilisation measurements may be immature. A short spike should not drive a long-lived capital decision. We should instrument the system, establish a baseline, and define in advance what would justify buying: sustained peak utilisation above a target, repeated SLO misses attributable to capacity rather than scheduling, memory pressure that cannot be resolved by routing or quantisation, and a forecast that remains above capacity after optimisation. Those triggers should be reviewed with finance and operations, not only engineering.

I recommend a ninety-day programme with a named owner, a capped budget, and success metrics covering cost per useful workload, p95 and p99 latency, queue delay, failure rate, and stranded capacity. The team should improve scheduling and packing, introduce or refine model routing and caching, validate reliability under degraded capacity, and document the remaining headroom. At the end of the quarter, we should revisit the purchase decision with data. If the triggers are met earlier, we should escalate rather than wait. This approach respects cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility, and it keeps the hardware decision grounded in evidence rather than anxiety about demand.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and AI Infrastructure Team  
**From:** Engineering Leadership  
**Subject:** Local AI capacity: improve utilisation before expanding hardware

We need to make a near-term decision about whether to buy additional local AI hardware or to invest first in getting more useful work out of the hardware we already own. My recommendation is to pursue a focused utilisation programme for the next quarter, with a pre-agreed evidence threshold and a reserved capital option to buy later if the data justifies it. This is not a permanent rejection of expansion. It is a sequencing decision that recognises how much uncertainty we still have about demand shape, workload mix, and the real cost of our current idle capacity.

The cost case is not simply the purchase price of additional accelerators. Local AI hardware carries power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare-part inventory, and depreciation costs, and those costs are incurred whether or not the hardware is busy. If our current utilisation is uneven, buying more capacity can make the average cost per useful inference worse rather than better. The utilisation programme should therefore start with measurement: per-device utilisation, queue wait times, batch sizes, model residency, memory pressure, and the proportion of requests that could be routed to smaller or quantised models. We should also distinguish interactive latency-sensitive traffic from batch or offline work, because those workloads have different tolerance for queueing and can often share the same hardware more efficiently.

Latency is the main reason we cannot simply maximise utilisation. Higher utilisation usually means longer queues and worse tail latency, and tail latency is what users notice. The goal is not to drive every device to saturation; it is to raise useful throughput while protecting service-level objectives. That may mean stricter admission control for interactive requests, separate scheduling pools for batch work, better batching policies, and model routing that sends simple requests to cheaper paths. If we can demonstrate that we can raise throughput without degrading p95 or p99 latency beyond agreed bounds, we will have created real capacity without new capital.

Reliability also argues for caution. Additional hardware can improve redundancy, but only if it is deployed with clear failure domains and spare capacity. Buying more devices without improving scheduling or observability can increase operational surface area without increasing resilience. Conversely, better utilisation can free up headroom for failover and maintenance windows. We should treat a modest reserve of capacity as a reliability requirement, not as waste, and measure utilisation against the capacity that is actually available for serving traffic after accounting for failure and maintenance margins.

The opportunity cost is significant. Capital spent on hardware is capital not spent on engineers, observability, model optimisation, or cloud burst capacity for rare peaks. A quarter of focused work on scheduling, batching, quantisation, caching, and workload placement is relatively cheap and highly reversible. Hardware procurement is much less reversible: lead times, depreciation, and integration work make it a commitment that is difficult to unwind if demand shifts or model architectures change. That asymmetry should bias us toward optimisation first, provided we set a clear deadline and do not let the programme become an excuse for indefinite delay.

My recommendation is therefore to approve a time-boxed utilisation effort with named owners, measurable targets, and a decision gate. The gate should include sustained utilisation, queue latency, error rates, and a forecast of demand under realistic growth scenarios. If we hit the targets and still see unacceptable latency or reliability risk, we should buy. If we cannot hit the targets, buying more hardware is likely to repeat the same inefficiency at larger scale. The uncertainty is real: demand may grow faster than expected, and some workloads may not be optimisable without hardware changes. That is why we should reserve the capital and define the trigger now, rather than treating this as a binary choice. Improve utilisation first, but keep the purchase option live and evidence-based.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Engineering Leadership  
**From:** Platform Engineering  
**Subject:** Local AI capacity: buy more hardware or improve utilisation?  
**Date:** [Date]

We need to decide whether to add local AI hardware or extract more capacity from the equipment we already own. The instinct to buy is understandable: demand is rising, queues are visible, and new GPUs promise immediate relief. But the decision is less about whether more capacity would help than about whether hardware is the cheapest, fastest, and most reversible way to get it. My recommendation is to fund a focused utilisation programme for the next quarter, hold the hardware purchase as a pre-approved but gated option, and buy only if sustained demand still exceeds capacity after we have removed scheduling, memory, and routing inefficiencies. This is not a rejection of hardware; it is a sequencing decision that preserves capital and keeps our options open.

The cost case is not simply capex versus engineering time. Local hardware carries depreciation, power, cooling, rack space, spare parts, and operational attention. Idle GPUs are expensive even when they are not running workloads, and average utilisation is a poor guide because it hides fragmentation, memory pressure, and tail latency. A cluster can look busy on average while specific models wait behind long-running jobs or fail to fit because memory is stranded across devices. Improving utilisation means better scheduling, batching where latency budgets allow, model routing to smaller or quantised variants, caching, multi-tenancy, and observability that distinguishes real capacity from apparent capacity. These changes cost engineering time, but they are usually cheaper than a new node and they compound across every future workload. The opportunity cost of buying too early is not just money; it is the engineering attention consumed by procurement, integration, and operations while simpler bottlenecks remain unfixed.

Latency and reliability cut both ways. More hardware can reduce queueing and provide redundancy, but only if the bottleneck is compute capacity rather than scheduling, data movement, or model configuration. Adding nodes to a poorly utilised cluster can increase operational surface area without improving p95 time-to-first-token or throughput. Conversely, aggressive utilisation improvements can harm latency if we over-pack devices or batch beyond interactive SLOs. We should therefore define explicit service-level objectives for interactive and batch workloads, measure queue depth and memory pressure rather than average utilisation alone, and preserve headroom for failover. Reliability also argues for caution: a utilisation programme that introduces complex preemption or shared tenancy can create new failure modes, so it needs fallback paths and clear ownership. Hardware purchases can improve failure domains, but they also add maintenance burden and spare-capacity requirements that are easy to underestimate.

Reversibility is the strongest argument for improving utilisation first. Software and scheduling changes can be rolled back, tuned, or abandoned; a hardware purchase is a multi-year commitment with lead times, depreciation, and vendor-specific constraints. Cloud burst capacity can serve as a temporary pressure valve for predictable peaks, though it must be priced against local marginal cost and data-egress constraints. A gated purchase also lets us pre-qualify vendors and reserve budget without committing before we understand whether the demand is durable or a short-lived spike.

There is real uncertainty here. Our forecasts are imperfect, some workloads may prove genuinely latency-sensitive and non-batchable, and utilisation data may be incomplete. The utilisation programme should therefore have a capped budget, a fixed review date, and measurable exit criteria: sustained queueing beyond agreed SLOs, memory pressure that cannot be resolved by routing or quantisation, and demand that remains above capacity after optimisation. If those thresholds are met, we should buy incrementally rather than in a single large commitment, preserving reversibility and matching capacity to observed need. If they are not met, we will have avoided an expensive purchase and gained a more efficient platform. My recommendation is clear: improve utilisation first, keep the hardware option warm, and let measured SLO pressure—not visible queues alone—trigger the purchase.

Internal Engineering Memo

To: Local AI Platform Team  
From: Engineering Lead  
Subject: Hardware expansion versus utilisation

We need to choose between buying more local AI hardware and getting more useful capacity out of the fleet we already own. My recommendation is to commit to a focused utilisation programme for the next quarter, with explicit performance and capacity exit criteria, and to treat additional hardware as a staged, evidence-driven purchase rather than the default response to current pressure. This is not a permanent refusal to buy. It is a sequencing decision that preserves capital and keeps our options open while we learn whether our bottleneck is really compute capacity or the way we schedule, batch, place, and operate the capacity we have.

The cost case is not just the purchase price of additional accelerators. More local hardware brings power and cooling load, rack space, spares, firmware and driver maintenance, monitoring, and the engineering attention needed to keep another failure domain healthy. Utilisation work also costs money, principally engineering time and some tooling, but it is usually smaller and it compounds: better scheduling, right-sizing, caching, model routing, and observability improve every future hardware purchase as well. We should measure cost per useful inference or training job, not cost per installed device, because idle or fragmented capacity is expensive even when it is already paid for.

Latency is the strongest argument for buying, but only if compute capacity is genuinely the constraint. If tail latency is driven by cold starts, poor model placement, oversized reservations, queueing behind long jobs, or inefficient batching, more hardware may add capacity without fixing the user experience. A good utilisation programme can reduce latency through better admission control, cache hits, right-sized models, and sensible concurrency. It can also make latency worse if we consolidate too aggressively or batch too eagerly, so we need service-level objectives for median and tail latency and the instrumentation to see queue time separately from execution time. We should not trade a visible hardware purchase for an invisible latency regression.

Reliability cuts both ways. Additional nodes increase failure domains, driver and firmware drift, power and cooling exposure, and operational burden on a small team. Utilisation improvements can improve reliability through standard images, health checks, graceful draining, and clearer capacity ownership, but consolidation can also remove redundancy. We should preserve headroom for critical services and avoid making one scheduler or one pool a single point of failure. The goal is not maximum occupancy at any cost; it is predictable service with enough slack to absorb failures and bursts.

Opportunity cost matters because capital and senior engineering time are both scarce. Money spent on hardware now cannot be spent on tooling, reliability work, or a later generation of hardware with better economics. Team time spent tuning utilisation is also an investment, but it produces reusable operational knowledge and is less lumpy than a hardware order. Lead times and vendor uncertainty further argue for keeping the decision reversible. Software and scheduling changes can be rolled back or adjusted quickly. A hardware purchase depreciates, consumes space and power, and is difficult to undo. If we need a bridge, a small incremental purchase, a lease, or cloud burst capacity is more reversible than a large local expansion.

I therefore recommend an eight-to-twelve-week utilisation programme with clear exit criteria. We should establish current useful throughput, queue delay, memory pressure, and latency SLO attainment; remove obvious fragmentation and idle reservations; improve scheduling and batching; and document the remaining gap at peak with reasonable failure headroom. If, after that work, we still cannot meet latency and reliability targets at forecast demand, we should buy incrementally, starting with the smallest reversible option that closes the measured gap. The uncertainty is real: forecasts may be wrong, utilisation metrics can hide fragmentation, and software gains may be smaller than hoped. That is exactly why the first move should be the reversible one.

appliance.kv_cache_dtype: as DeepSeek's reference caches it: sliding-window KV in FP8 E4M3 with a UE8M0 scale per 32, compressed (indexed) KV in FP4 E2M1 with an E4M3 scale per 16, MXFP4 indexer keys
appliance.negotiated_link_speed: 200 Gb/s per ConnectX-7 port (4 cables, 8 RDMA paths)
appliance.quantisation: the native checkpoint, not requantized: block-32 FP8 E4M3 dense weights (a UE8M0 scale per 32x32), MXFP4 (E2M1) routed experts, BF16 router gate, indexer head weights and compressor; MXFP8 activations where DeepSeek's reference quantizes them
appliance.scheduler: max sequences 16; max batched tokens 8192; chunked prefill; asynchronous scheduling; prefix caching; CUDA graphs FULL_AND_PIECEWISE
appliance.server_sampling_defaults: temperature 1.0, top_p 1.0 for requests that set none
appliance.serving_engine: vLLM: Local Inference Lab integration/karmic-kraken-beta 19f2c20e with the spark-ds41f patch series (patch head c001cc4e, tree d11e9836); TileLang 0.1.15 kernels, DeepSeek TileKernels 2.0.0, sparknet one-shot RoCE collectives
